title: Fed Ground
subtitle: What blood grows
text: Ground that blood reaches grows faster, and the gourd grows nowhere else: its vine will not put on a leaf in dry soil, and bone meal will not wake it. There are three ways to feed a crop, each smaller and dearer than the last. A scab spike hanging under a ceiling drips when fresh blood stands just above its root, in the block it hangs from or in a basin, a machine or a wet gutter on that block. It takes only blood whoever hung it may draw, theirs or their bloodline's; a spike nobody hung drinks only from a tank nobody owns. Each drop takes a few millilitres and feeds the soil it lands on and the ring round it for about five minutes, so a ceiling of spikes over a field is a slow, wide farm; a fed spike now and then grows longer. A wet stain beside a crop's soil feeds it the same way, briefly. A planting basin is a bed of soil over a small tank: fill it by hand or run a worked gutter past it, and while its blood is fresh the plant in it, and the soil beside it, grow far faster, a few millilitres for each extra growth; a stem in a basin still sets its fruit on dirt or farmland beside it, as in a field. It clots like any tank, and what sets comes out as Formations. Under the Mycelial Lantern's bell, seeds set in the culture slot grow a stage every thirty seconds for twenty-five millilitres, and a ripe crop goes to the output and is sown again; spores still fruit their enzymes there. A spike dripping into an empty cauldron turns it into a Sanguine Condenser and lets each drop set there; that Condenser belongs to whoever keeps the tank the drops came from, and once it has given up all it held it goes back to plain iron. Sculpting, Projection, with Vital Effusion selected: hold the verb on a plant that bone meal could grow and blood soaks its soil and grows it, a step a second. Spores planted on their own wood are fed the same ways; see Strain Beds.
